So the men went and traveled through the land, and they recorded it in a book, city by city, in seven divisions. Then they returned to Joshua in the camp at Shiloh.
Joshua cast lots for them at Shiloh before Yahweh. There Joshua apportioned the land to the Israelites according to their divisions.
The lot for the tribe of Benjamin’s descendants{b} came up, by their clans, and the territory assigned to them lay between the descendants of Judah and of Joseph.
Their northern boundary started at the Jordan, climbed to the slope north of Jericho, then went up west through the hill country and ended at the wilderness of Beth-aven.
From there the border crossed south toward Luz, to Luz’s slope (that is, Bethel), and descended to Ataroth-addar, on the hill south of Lower Beth-horon.

Then the boundary turned and curved along the west side toward the south, from the hill facing Beth-horon on the south, and finished at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), a city of Judah’s descendants. That was the western side.
The southern side began at the outskirts of Kiriath-jearim. The border went out westward{c} and went to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah.

The border descended to the foot of the mountain facing the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, at the north end of the Valley of Rephaim, ran down the Hinnom Valley along the Jebusite’s southern slope, and reached En-rogel.
Then it bent in a northerly direction, going out to En-shemesh, and from there to Geliloth, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim. Then it went down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben,
passed on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-arabah,{d} and went down to the Arabah.
The border continued north of the slope of Beth-hoglah and ended at the Salt Sea’s northern inlet, at the Jordan’s southern end. That was the southern boundary.
The Jordan bounded it on the east. This was the inheritance of Benjamin’s descendants by their clans, with its boundaries all around.
The cities of the tribe of Benjamin, by their clans, were Jericho, Beth-hoglah, and Emek-keziz,
also Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, and Bethel,
also Avvim, Parah, and Ophrah,
and Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, and Geba—twelve cities and their villages.
Gibeon, Ramah,{e} Beeroth,
Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah,
Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah,
Zela, Haeleph, the Jebusite city (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeath,{f} and Kiriath{g}—fourteen cities and their villages. This was the inheritance of Benjamin’s descendants, by their clans.

notes.text: Shiloh may mean “place of rest” or “tranquility.” It became the site of the sanctuary through the period of the judges (1 Samuel 1–4).
Benjamin means “son of the right hand” or “son of the south” (Genesis 35:18).
Or “to the west.” The text is difficult; the Septuagint reads “to Gasin.”
The Hebrew reads “to the shoulder opposite the Arabah.” Some ancient witnesses read “Beth-arabah,” as in 15:6.
Ramah means “height.”
Gibeath means “hill.” This is probably Gibeah, Saul’s town (1 Samuel 10:26).
Hebrew Qiryat, “city.” Some propose reading Kiriath-jearim, but 18:14 assigns that city to Judah.

verses.text: The second lot fell to Simeon,{a} to the tribe of Simeon’s descendants by their clans, and their inheritance lay within the inheritance of Judah’s descendants.
Their inheritance included Beersheba, Sheba,{b} and Moladah,
also Hazar-shual, Balah, and Ezem,
also Eltolad, Bethul, and Hormah,
also Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, and Hazar-susah,
also Beth-lebaoth and Sharuhen—thirteen cities and their villages;
Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan: four cities with their villages,
as well as all the villages around these cities up to Baalath-beer, Ramah in the Negev. This was the inheritance of Simeon’s tribe, by their clans.
Simeon’s inheritance was taken from Judah’s territory, because Judah’s portion was too large for them; so the Simeonites received their inheritance within Judah’s.
The third lot came up for Zebulun’s descendants,{c} by their clans. Their inherited territory extended to Sarid.
Then their border went up westward and on to Maralah, touched Dabbesheth, then the brook that is east of Jokneam.
From Sarid it went in the other direction eastward toward the sunrise to the border of Chisloth-tabor. From there it went to Daberath, then up to Japhia.
From there it crossed eastward, toward the sunrise, to Gath-hepher and Eth-kazin, and continued to Rimmon, where it curved toward Neah.
Then on the north the border turned about to Hannathon, and it ended at the Valley of Iphtahel,
with Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem{d}—twelve cities and their villages.
That was the inheritance of Zebulun’s descendants by their clans—these cities and their villages.
The fourth lot fell to Issachar,{e} to Issachar’s descendants by their clans.
Their territory included Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem,
Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath,
Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez,
Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez.
The border also touched Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth-shemesh, and their border ended at the Jordan: sixteen cities with their villages.
That was the inheritance of Issachar’s tribe by their clans—the cities and their villages.
The fifth lot fell to the tribe of Asher’s descendants{f} by their clans.
Their territory included Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph,
also Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal. On the west it reached Carmel{g} and Shihor-libnath.
Then it turned east toward Beth-dagon, reached Zebulun and the Valley of Iphtahel, and went north to Beth-emek and Neiel, continuing north to Cabul,
Ebron,{h} Rehob, Hammon, and Kanah, as far as Great Sidon.
Then the border turned toward Ramah and the fortified city of Tyre.{i} It then turned to Hosah and ended at the sea; there were also Mahalab,{j} Achzib,
Ummah, Aphek, and Rehob: twenty-two cities with their villages.
That was the inheritance of Asher’s tribe by their clans—these cities and their villages.
The sixth lot fell to Naphtali’s descendants,{k} by their clans.
Their border ran from Heleph and the oak at Zaanannim, with Adami-nekeb and Jabneel, to Lakkum, and ended at the Jordan.
Then the border turned westward to Aznoth-tabor and went from there to Hukkok, touching Zebulun on the south and Asher on the west and Judah{l} at the Jordan on the east.
The fortified cities were Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth,
Adamah, Ramah, Hazor,
Kedesh, Edrei, En-hazor,
Yiron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh: nineteen cities with their villages.
That was the inheritance of Naphtali’s tribe by their clans—the cities and their villages.
The seventh lot fell to Dan’s tribe{m} by their clans.
Their inherited territory included Zorah, Eshtaol, and Ir-shemesh,
also Shaalabbin, Aijalon, and Ithlah,
also Elon, Timnah, and Ekron,
also Eltekeh, Gibbethon, and Baalath,
also Jehud, Bene-berak, and Gath-rimmon,
and Me-jarkon and Rakkon with the territory over against Joppa.

When the territory of the Danites slipped from them,{n} the Danites went up, fought against Leshem, took it, and put it to the sword; they occupied it and lived there, and they called Leshem “Dan,” after the name of their ancestor Dan.
That was the inheritance of Dan’s tribe by their clans—these cities and their villages.
After they had finished distributing the lands as inheritances, the Israelites gave Joshua son of Nun an inheritance among them.
By command of Yahweh they gave him the city that he asked for, Timnath-serah{o} in the hill country of Ephraim. He rebuilt the city and settled in it.

These are the inheritances that Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the family heads of the tribes of Israel distributed by lot at Shiloh, before Yahweh, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. So they completed the dividing of the land.

notes.text: Simeon means “heard” (Genesis 29:33).
Or “Shema,” as in 15:26 and 1 Chronicles 4:28; the list totals thirteen only if Sheba is a repetition of Beersheba.
Zebulun may mean “honor” or “dwelling” (Genesis 30:20).
This is a Bethlehem in Galilee, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) northwest of Nazareth, not Bethlehem of Judah.
Issachar sounds like the Hebrew for “there is a reward” (Genesis 30:18).
Asher means “happy” or “blessed” (Genesis 30:13).
Carmel means “garden land” or “orchard.”
Some Hebrew manuscripts read Abdon (compare 21:30).
Tyre (Hebrew Tsor) means “rock.”
Hebrew “from Hebel”; the reading Mahalab, a town known from Assyrian records, involves a slight change.
Naphtali means “my wrestling” (Genesis 30:8).
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint lacks “and Judah.” The phrase may refer to Jair’s towns east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 2:21–23), or the text may be damaged.
Dan means “he judged” or “judge” (Genesis 30:6).

Literally “went out from them.” The Septuagint has a different text in verses 47–48. It says that the Amorites pressed the Danites into the hill country and did not let them come down into the valley, that the Danites took Lachish (the Hebrew has Leshem) and called it Lasendan, and that the Amorites stayed in Edom and Shaalbim until Ephraim made them pay tribute. Compare Judges 1:34–35; 18:27–29.

Timnath-serah means “portion that remains” (or “extra portion”). Judges 2:9 calls it Timnath-heres, “portion of the sun,” and Serah may be a deliberate reversal of the letters. The Septuagint spells it Thamnasarach.

verses.text: Then Yahweh spoke to Joshua, saying,
“Speak to the Israelites, saying, ‘Appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses,
so that the manslayer who strikes any person unintentionally, without knowing it, may flee there. They are to be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood.{a}

He shall flee to one of these cities, stand at the entrance of its gate, and state his case to that city’s elders. They shall then bring him into the city, give him a place, and he shall live among them.{b}
If the avenger of blood pursues him, they are not to give up the manslayer into his hand, because he struck his neighbor without knowing it and did not hate him in the past.

He must live in that city until the assembly has judged his case, and until the high priest serving at that time has died. Only then may the killer return to the town from which he fled, to his own home.’”
So they set apart Kedesh{c} in Galilee{d} in the hill country of Naphtali, Shechem{e} in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah.

On the east side of the Jordan, opposite Jericho, they set apart Bezer, in the wilderness on the tableland, belonging to Reuben; Ramoth in Gilead, belonging to Gad; and Golan in Bashan, belonging to Manasseh.

These were the cities set aside for all the Israelites, and for the foreign resident among them, so that anyone who killed a person accidentally could flee there and not be killed by the avenger of blood before standing trial before the congregation.

notes.text: Hebrew go’el haddam, the nearest relative, whose duty was to take responsibility for a family member’s death. The same word go’el means “redeemer” elsewhere (Ruth 4:1–6).

The Septuagint lacks verses 4–6 and the phrase “without knowing it” in verse 3. In verse 3 it reads instead, “until he stands before the congregation for judgment.” The longer Hebrew text echoes Deuteronomy 19:1–13, while the shorter Greek text echoes Numbers 35:9–28.
Kedesh means “holy place.”
Galilee (Hebrew Galil) means “circle” or “district.”
Shechem means “shoulder” or “ridge,” perhaps from its position on the saddle between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.

verses.text: Then the heads of the fathers’ houses of the Levites came to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers’ houses of the tribes of the Israelites.
At Shiloh in the land of Canaan they told them, “Yahweh commanded through Moses that we be given towns to live in, with pastureland for our livestock.”
So by command of Yahweh the Israelites gave to the Levites from their inheritance these cities and their pasturelands.
The first lot fell to the Kohathite clans. The Levites who were descendants of Aaron the priest received thirteen cities by lot from the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin.
The remaining Kohathites received ten cities by lot from the clans of Ephraim, from Dan, and from half of Manasseh.
The Gershonites received thirteen cities by lot from the clans of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan.
The Merarites, by their clans, received twelve cities from Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun.
The Israelites gave these cities with their pastures to the Levites by lot, as Yahweh had commanded through Moses.
From the tribes of Judah and Simeon they gave these cities, listed by name,
which went to Aaron’s descendants, of the Kohathite clans of Levi’s descendants, since the first lot was theirs.
They gave them Kiriath-arba (Arba was the father of Anak), that is, Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, with the pasturelands around it.
The fields around the city and its villages, however, were given to Caleb son of Jephunneh as his own.
To Aaron the priest’s descendants they gave Hebron, a city of refuge for the killer, with its pastures, along with Libnah and its pastures,
Jattir with its pasturelands, Eshtemoa with its pasturelands,
Holon with its pasturelands, Debir with its pasturelands,
Ain,{a} Juttah, and Beth-shemesh, each with its pastures—nine cities from these two tribes.
Then out of the tribe of Benjamin: Gibeon with its pasturelands, Geba with its pasturelands,
Anathoth{b} with its pasturelands, and Almon with its pasturelands: four cities.
Altogether the cities of Aaron’s descendants, the priests, were thirteen cities with their pastures.
As for the remaining Kohathite clans of the Levites, their allotted cities came from the tribe of Ephraim.
They were given Shechem, a city of refuge for the killer, with its pastures in the hill country of Ephraim, and Gezer with its pastures,
Kibzaim with its pasturelands, Beth-horon with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the tribe of Dan: Elteke and Gibbethon, each with its pastures,
Aijalon with its pasturelands, Gath-rimmon with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the half-tribe of Manasseh: Taanach and Gath-rimmon,{c} each with its pastures—two cities.
In all, the cities for the clans of the remaining Kohathites were ten, with their pastures.
To the Gershonites, a Levite clan, they gave from the half-tribe of Manasseh: Golan in Bashan, a city of refuge for the killer, and Be-eshterah,{d} each with its pastures—two cities.
From the tribe of Issachar: Kishion and Daberath, each with its pastures,
Jarmuth with its pasturelands, En-gannim with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the tribe of Asher: Mishal and Abdon, each with its pastures,
Helkath with its pasturelands, and Rehob with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the tribe of Naphtali: Kedesh in Galilee, a city of refuge for the killer, Hammoth-dor, and Kartan, each with its pastures—three cities.
Altogether the cities of the Gershonite clans were thirteen, with their pastures.
To the rest of the Levites, the Merarite clans, they gave from the tribe of Zebulun: Jokneam and Kartah, each with its pastures,
Dimnah with its pasturelands, Nahalal with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the tribe of Reuben:{e} Bezer and Jahaz, each with its pastures,
Kedemoth with its pasturelands, and Mephaath with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the tribe of Gad: Ramoth in Gilead, a city of refuge for the killer, and Mahanaim, each with its pastures,
Heshbon and Jazer, each with its pastures—four cities in all.
All the cities allotted to the Merarite clans, the rest of the Levite families, came to twelve.
The cities of the Levites in the midst of the possession of the Israelites were in all forty-eight cities with their pasturelands.
Each of these cities had pastureland surrounding it; this was true of all of them.{f}
So Yahweh gave Israel all the land he had sworn to give their fathers, and they took possession of it and settled in it.
Yahweh gave them rest on every side just as he had sworn to their fathers. Not one of all their enemies had withstood them, for Yahweh had given all their enemies into their hands.
Of all the good promises Yahweh had made to the house of Israel, not one word failed; every one came true.

notes.text: Ain means “spring.” The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 6:59 read Ashan.
Anathoth was later the hometown of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:1).
The repetition of Gath-rimmon from verse 24 is probably a copying error. 1 Chronicles 6:70 has Bileam (that is, Ibleam), and the Septuagint reads Iebatha.
Be-eshterah is probably a contraction of Beth-ashtarah, “house of Astarte.” 1 Chronicles 6:71 has Ashtaroth.

Verses 36–37 are lacking in many Hebrew manuscripts and in some printed editions of the Hebrew Bible, though the edition followed here includes them. They are present in the Septuagint and in 1 Chronicles 6:78–79, and the totals in verses 7 and 40 (twelve cities) require them.

The Septuagint adds, “And Joshua finished dividing the land by its borders. And the Israelites gave a portion to Joshua by the command of the Lord. They gave him the city that he asked for, Thamnasachar in the hill country of Ephraim. And Joshua built the city and lived in it. And Joshua took the flint knives with which he had circumcised the Israelites who were born in the wilderness on the way, and put them in Thamnasachar.” Compare 19:49–50 and 24:31 (Septuagint).

verses.text: Then Joshua summoned the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh
and said to them, “You have kept all that Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, and you have obeyed my voice in all that I have commanded you.
All these many days, up to this day, you have not abandoned your brothers, but have kept the charge Yahweh your God gave you.

And now Yahweh your God has given rest to your brothers, as he promised them. Therefore turn now and go to your tents, to the land of your possession, which Moses the servant of Yahweh gave you beyond the Jordan.

Only be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, to love Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.”
So Joshua blessed them and sent them away, and they went to their tents.

To one half of the tribe of Manasseh Moses had given land in Bashan, while to the other half Joshua gave land alongside their brothers west of the Jordan. When Joshua sent them home to their tents and blessed them,

he said to them, “Go back to your tents with great wealth and with very much livestock, with silver, gold, bronze, and iron, and with very many garments. Divide the spoil of your enemies with your brothers.”

So the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh left the Israelites at Shiloh in the land of Canaan and went back to Gilead, the land they owned, which they had taken by Yahweh’s command through Moses.

When they reached the district{a} of the Jordan in the land of Canaan, the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh built an altar there beside the Jordan, an altar that was impressive in size.
The Israelites were told, “The Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh have built an altar at the border of Canaan, in the Jordan district, on the side that faces the Israelites.”
When the Israelites heard this, the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh to go to war against them.
Then the Israelites sent to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, Phinehas{b} the son of Eleazar the priest,
and with him ten chiefs, one from each of the fathers’ houses of each of the tribes of Israel, every one of them the head of a fathers’ house among the clans{c} of Israel.
They came to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, and they said to them,

“This is the word of the whole congregation of Yahweh: ‘What is this unfaithfulness you have shown toward the God of Israel, turning away today from following Yahweh by building yourselves an altar and rebelling against Yahweh today?
Was the iniquity of Peor{d} too little for us, from which we are not yet cleansed to this day, though a plague struck the congregation of Yahweh,
that you too must turn away this day from following Yahweh? If you too rebel against Yahweh today, then tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel.

Yet if you find the land you hold to be unclean, then cross to Yahweh’s own land, where his tabernacle stands, and settle among us. But never rebel against Yahweh, nor make us rebels, by raising an altar for yourselves apart from the altar of Yahweh our God.
Did not Achan son of Zerah act unfaithfully regarding what was set apart for destruction, so that wrath fell on the whole congregation of Israel? He was not the only one to die for his iniquity.’”
The Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh answered the heads of the families of Israel:
“The Mighty One, God, Yahweh! The Mighty One, God, Yahweh!{e} He knows, and Israel too shall know! If this was rebellion or unfaithfulness toward Yahweh, do not save us today
by building an altar to turn away from Yahweh. And if our purpose was to offer on it burnt offerings, grain offerings, or peace offerings, may Yahweh himself require an account.
No! We acted from a worry that in days to come your children would say to our children, ‘What business do you have with Yahweh, the God of Israel?
For Yahweh has made the Jordan a boundary between us and you, you Reubenites and Gadites. You have no portion in Yahweh.’ So your children might make our children cease to fear Yahweh.
That is why we said, ‘Let us get ready to build an altar—not for burnt offering and not for sacrifice,

but to be a witness between you and us, and between our generations after us, that we do serve Yahweh before him with our burnt offerings, our sacrifices, and our peace offerings; then your children will not be able to tell our children in days to come, “You have no share in Yahweh.”’

And we thought, ‘If they ever say this to us or to our descendants in the future, we will reply, “See the likeness of Yahweh’s altar, which our fathers built, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between you and us.”’

Far be it from us that we should rebel against Yahweh and turn away this day from following Yahweh by building an altar for burnt offering, grain offering, or sacrifice, other than the altar of Yahweh our God that stands before his tabernacle!”
When Phinehas the priest, with the leaders of the congregation, the heads of Israel’s families who were with him, heard the words spoken by the Reubenites, Gadites, and Manassites, it pleased them.

Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest told the Reubenites, Gadites, and Manassites, “Today we know that Yahweh is among us, since you have not committed this act of unfaithfulness against Yahweh. You have now rescued the Israelites from Yahweh’s hand.”
Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest and the leaders then turned back from the Reubenites and Gadites in Gilead and returned to Canaan, to the Israelites, and gave them the report.
The report pleased the Israelites, and they blessed God. They said no more about going to war to destroy the land in which the Reubenites and Gadites lived.
The Reubenites and Gadites named the altar Witness,{f} saying, “It is a witness between us that Yahweh is God.”

notes.text: Hebrew gelilot, “circles” or “districts,” possibly a place name, Geliloth; so in verse 11. The Septuagint reads “Galaad” (Gilead).
Phinehas is an Egyptian name, probably meaning “the Nubian” (Numbers 25:7).
Hebrew “thousands,” a term for clan divisions; so in verses 21 and 30.
See Numbers 25:1–9.
Hebrew El Elohim Yahweh, three names for God, repeated as a solemn oath.

Hebrew ‘ed, “witness.” The name is not in the standard Hebrew text, which reads “called the altar, ‘For it is a witness…’” Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac supply it. The Septuagint reads, “Joshua gave a name to the altar… and said, ‘It is a witness in the midst of them.’”

verses.text: Long afterward, when Yahweh had given Israel rest from all their enemies around them, and Joshua had grown old and was well along in years,
Joshua called together all Israel—its elders, heads, judges, and officers—and told them, “I am old and well along in years.
You have seen all that Yahweh your God has done to all these nations for your sake, for it is Yahweh your God who has fought for you.
Look, I have assigned to you, as an inheritance for your tribes, the nations that remain, as well as all the nations I have cut off, from the Jordan to the Great Sea on the west.
Yahweh your God himself will thrust them out from before you and drive them away from you, and you will take possession of their land, as Yahweh your God promised you.
So be very strong to keep and do everything written in the book of the law of Moses, without turning from it to the right or to the left,
so that you do not mingle with these nations left among you, mention the names of their gods, swear by them, serve them, or bow down to them,
but you are to cling to Yahweh your God just as you have done to this day.
For Yahweh has driven out great and mighty nations ahead of you; as for you, up to this day no one has withstood you.
A single one of you chases a thousand, because Yahweh your God is the one fighting for you, as he promised you.
Be very careful, therefore, for your own sakes, to love Yahweh your God.
For if you turn away and hold fast to the survivors of these nations that remain among you, and intermarry with them and mix with them and they with you,

know for certain that Yahweh your God will not go on driving these nations out ahead of you. They will become snares and traps for you, whips on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from this good land Yahweh your God has given you.

“I am now about to go the way of all the earth. All of you know in your hearts and souls that not one of all the good things Yahweh your God spoke concerning you has failed. Everything has come true for you; not one of them has failed.

But just as every good thing Yahweh your God promised you has come to you, so Yahweh will bring on you every evil thing until he has wiped you out from this good land that Yahweh your God has given you,

if you break the covenant of Yahweh your God that he commanded you, and go serve other gods and bow down to them. Then Yahweh’s anger will burn against you, and you will quickly perish from the good land he has given you.”{a}

notes.text: The Septuagint lacks the last sentence of this verse (“Then the anger of Yahweh…”).

verses.text: Joshua assembled all the tribes of Israel at Shechem{a} and called for the elders, heads, judges, and officers of Israel, and they stood before God.

Joshua told all the people, “Here is what Yahweh, Israel’s God, declares: ‘In ancient times your fathers lived on the other side of the River,{b} namely Terah, the father of Abraham and the father of Nahor, and they served other gods.
But I took your father Abraham from beyond the River, led him through the whole land of Canaan, and multiplied his offspring. I gave him Isaac.
To Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau; to Esau I gave Mount Seir’s hill country as a possession, while Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt.
Then I sent Moses and Aaron, and I struck Egypt with what I did in its midst, and afterward I brought you out.{c}
I brought your fathers out of Egypt, and you came to the sea. The Egyptians pursued your fathers with chariots and horsemen to the Red Sea.

When they cried out to Yahweh, he put darkness between you and the Egyptians, and brought the sea down over them and covered them. Your eyes witnessed what I did to the Egyptians. Afterward you stayed for many days in the wilderness.
I brought you into the land of the Amorites who lived east of the Jordan; they fought against you, but I handed them over to you, and you took their land, and I destroyed them ahead of you.
Then Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and fought against Israel. He sent and called Balaam the son of Beor to curse you,
but I refused to listen to Balaam, so he actually blessed you, and I rescued you from his hand.

You went over the Jordan and reached Jericho; Jericho’s leaders{d} fought you, and so did the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites, and Jebusites, but I delivered them into your hand.
I sent the hornet{e} ahead of you, and it drove out the two kings of the Amorites{f} before you—not by your sword or your bow.
I gave you a land you had not tilled and cities you had not built; you now live in them and eat from vineyards and olive orchards that you never planted.’
“So now fear Yahweh and serve him with integrity and faithfulness. Throw away the gods your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve Yahweh.

But if serving Yahweh seems wrong to you, choose today whom you will serve: the gods your fathers served beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living. As for me and my household, we will serve Yahweh.”
Then the people answered, “Far be it from us that we should forsake Yahweh to serve other gods,

For it is Yahweh our God who brought up both us and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery, who performed those great signs before our eyes and kept us safe throughout the journey we made and among every nation we passed through.
Yahweh also drove all the peoples out ahead of us, namely the Amorites who lived in this land. We too, therefore, will serve Yahweh, for he is our God.”
But Joshua said to the people, “You are not able to serve Yahweh, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God. He will not forgive your transgressions or your sins.
If you forsake Yahweh and serve foreign gods, then he will turn and do you harm and consume you, after having done you good.”
The people said to Joshua, “No, but we will serve Yahweh.”
Then Joshua said to the people, “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen Yahweh, to serve him.” And they said, “We are witnesses.”
He said, “Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to Yahweh, the God of Israel.”
The people answered Joshua, “We will serve Yahweh our God and obey his voice.”
That day Joshua made a covenant with the people, and at Shechem{g} he set statutes and ordinances before them.
Joshua wrote these words in the Book of the Law of God. And he took a large stone and set it up there under the oak{h} that was by the sanctuary of Yahweh.
Joshua told all the people, “Look, this stone will witness against us, for it has heard all the words Yahweh spoke to us; it will witness against you if you are false to your God.”
So Joshua sent the people away, every man to his inheritance.
After these things Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Yahweh, died, being 110 years old.{i}
They buried him within his own inheritance at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.{j}
Israel served Yahweh all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and had known all the work that Yahweh did for Israel.{k}

Joseph’s bones, which the Israelites had carried up from Egypt, were buried at Shechem in the parcel of land that Jacob had purchased from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred pieces of money;{l} it became an inheritance for Joseph’s descendants.
Eleazar son of Aaron also died, and he was buried at Gibeah,{m} the property of his son Phinehas, who had been granted it in Ephraim’s hill country.{n}

notes.text: The Septuagint reads Shiloh here and in verse 25. Shechem was the site of Abraham’s first altar in the land (Genesis 12:6–7) and of Jacob’s burial of foreign gods (Genesis 35:4).
That is, the Euphrates; so in verses 3, 14, and 15.
The Septuagint has a shorter text in verses 5–7. It lacks “I sent Moses and Aaron” and some other phrases.
Hebrew ba‘ale, “the lords” or “citizens.”
Or “panic” or “terror” (Hebrew tsir‘ah). Compare Exodus 23:28 and Deuteronomy 7:20.
The Septuagint reads “twelve kings of the Amorites.” The Hebrew “two kings” refers to Sihon and Og (2:10).
The Septuagint reads “at Shiloh, before the tabernacle of the God of Israel.”
Or “terebinth,” a large tree. Compare Genesis 35:4, where Jacob hid foreign gods under the oak near Shechem.
An age of 110 years was considered the ideal life span in Egypt. Joseph died at the same age (Genesis 50:26).
Gaash may mean “quaking” or “shaking.”

The Septuagint places this verse before Joshua’s death (as verse 29). After the burial account it adds that Joshua’s flint blades, used to circumcise the Israelites at Gilgal once he had led them out of Egypt, were laid beside him in his grave, just as the Lord had commanded, and that they remain there to this day. Compare the Septuagint addition at 21:42.

Hebrew “for a hundred qesitah,” a unit of uncertain value, perhaps a weight of silver; it appears elsewhere only in Genesis 33:19 and Job 42:11. The Septuagint reads “for a hundred ewe-lambs.” Compare Genesis 33:19; Acts 7:16.
Gibeah means “hill.” The Septuagint reads Gabaar.

The Septuagint adds a longer ending: “On that day the Israelites took the ark of God and carried it around among them. And Phinehas served as priest in place of Eleazar his father until he died, and he was buried in his own place, Gabaar. And the Israelites went away, each to his own place and to his own city. And the Israelites worshiped Astarte and Ashtaroth and the gods of the nations around them. And the Lord gave them into the hands of Eglon king of Moab, and he ruled over them eighteen years.” This addition links the book to Judges 2:6–13 and 3:12–14.
